The Internet Archive scan was checked against its title page and against the rendered leaves containing Bhāskara's zero rules and Brahmagupta's algorithm. Colebrooke's nineteenth-century English is itself a historical translation layer: its “cipher,” “affirmative,” and “negative” are quotation-ready as this edition's words, not as a critical settlement of the Sanskrit. Brahmagupta's rules place zero among positive and negative quantities in addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, powers, and roots. Bhāskara's rules preserve a zero-denominator expression and then compare its invariance under finite addition or subtraction with divine immutability. It lets the source teach why the collapse proof is decisive inside ordinary field assumptions while refusing the further claim that every historical zero-denominator practice was merely meaningless. **Claim boundary:** Dutta offers a mathematically revisionist defence and modern analogies, not a critical edition of Brahmagupta or Bhāskara. In the zero–subject historical braid, Dutta prevents the formal limit from being falsified into an elementary prohibition: zero-divided expressions make the algebraic regime and its excluded operations visible.
